entries.title: Mallory McMorrow Wants Democrats to ‘Stop Looking at Polling’
entries.summary: The Michigan Democrat blamed a fake poll for contributing to a “death spiral” for her failed Senate campaign.
entries.content:
A Michigan Democrat, state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, is calling for polling and election reform after a fake polling firm revealed that it fabricated data throughout this election cycle.

McMorrow ran in the U.S. Senate primary in Michigan, eventually dropping out as she seemed to fade while Abdul El-Sayed, who is now the Democratic nominee, and Rep. Haley Stevens gained momentum. McMorrow blamed the fake poll for contributing to a “death spiral” for her campaign.

“If Democrats take a lesson away from this cycle, we have to fix this entire system,” McMorrow told The Washington Sun on Wednesday. “This is just one of many things that I think has made politics toxic for people, and we’ve got to restore trust. That's what this is about. People don't know what to trust.”

Less than two weeks out from Election Day, polling in many parts of the country appear to favor Democrats. But McMorrow is using the fake poll to warn Democrats against growing complacent.

“I think the biggest thing that I want to remind people now is, we shouldn't trust any polls,” McMorrow said. “There are two weeks left, so I don't want anybody to take anything for granted, which is why I've been calling for people to sign up for a canvassing shift, do whatever you can, because I hope this teaches us a lesson.”

In Michigan, polling shows a competitive race between El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers. It’s one of the most closely watched Senate races, and it’s playing out in a battleground state.

Wedgewood Polls, the fake polling firm, said in a statement posted to X on Tuesday that most of its midterm election polling was fabricated. The statement said it was conducting an “experiment” to expose issues with the polling industry.

The announcement came hours before FiftyPlusOne, an election analysis hub, released an investigation into Wedgewood Polls, indicating its methodology and data had “red flags.”

Wedgewood released polls on competitive races like the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary and Senate races in Nebraska, Alaska and Mississippi. Its data was cited by several major outlets and aggregation hubs.

“Our races come down to a handful of votes, and I want everybody to lay it all on the line,” McMorrow said. “My advice to everybody is stop looking at polling and go knock on some doors.”
entries.author: Ellie Fivas

entries.title: Judge Restricts Federal Agents’ Ability to Question Suspected Noncitizen Voters at Their Homes
entries.summary: Federal agents were allowed to knock on doors to ask residents in nine states about their immigration status and voting history.
entries.content:
A federal judge in California restricted the Department of Homeland Security’s authority to send federal agents to question people at their homes about their immigration status and voting history, saying the department is using unreliable data to do so.

In the weeks ahead of the midterms, President Donald Trump’s administration has ramped up efforts to crack down on what it claims is widespread voter fraud, despite noncitizen voting being extremely rare. In late August, DHS directed hundreds of immigration agents to pause their normal duties to search for evidence of noncitizen voting, according to whistleblower reports.

In the Wednesday order, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, a Joe Biden appointee, also found that DHS’s fraud crackdown likely violates voting-rights protections by frightening eligible citizens out of participating in the midterms.

Threats have already caused members of the California Nurses Association — which is suing DHS and Secretary Markwayne Mullin — to “withdraw from participating in electoral activity because they reasonably fear being subjected to physical, legal, or reputational harm to themselves and their loved ones,” Martínez-Olguín wrote.

The injunction covers the nine states DHS targeted in its operation: California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. The order restricts election-related field operations and interviews that could involve people agents know or reasonably should suspect are U.S. citizens.

The order focuses on a “voluminous and unreliable” list of potential targets — data that includes 48.2 million records that DHS received through independent sources “of questionable provenance,” Martínez-Olguín wrote, and another 50.6 million records from official state voter-roll data or from unreliable commercial versions of voter-roll data.

The California Nurses Association argues the data is being used to “surveil, covertly infiltrate, and interrogate the staff of non-profits and churches conducting voter engagement” for purposes of carrying out the campaign.

DHS-led doorknocking investigations have ramped up since September.

Martínez-Olguín said that the public’s interest in safe elections, free from interference or intimidation, “far exceed Defendants’ purported interest in combating unlawful voting by non-U.S. citizens.”

“Defendants announced the deployment of armed officers in a militarized action to individuals’ homes and communities during the final months before midterm elections, inspiring fear in the CNA/NNU members who wish to mobilize, educate, and assist voters,” she added.

California has been involved in a separate legal battle with the Justice Department, which tried to force the state to halt or set aside 20,000 ballots from potential noncitizen voters. State officials called the agency’s latest interrogations “voter suppression.” Tensions continued to rise after federal agents arrested dozens of green-card holders on allegations they sought illegal voter registrations.
entries.author: Gavin J. Quinton

entries.title: Roger Marshall Warns That the Senate Majority Runs ‘Through Kansas’
entries.summary: In a debate Wednesday, the Kansas Republican argued relentlessly that a vote for his opponent is a vote for Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader.
entries.content:
Sen. Roger Marshall acknowledged in a debate Wednesday that his Kansas seat, typically a lock for Republicans, could end up swinging control of the Senate.

Marshall is in a surprisingly tough reelection campaign against Democrat Adam Hamilton, with polls indicating a tight race. The state voted for Trump in 2024 by 16 percentage points and hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, yet Republicans — including President Donald Trump, who traveled to the state on Monday — have launched an all-out rescue mission for Marshall.

“Control of the Senate comes through Kansas,” Marshall said at the debate.

Marshall balanced a call for President Donald Trump’s voters to rally around him with critiques about the administration’s policies.

“I've had multiple times when I've objected to the president before,” Marshall said. “But I do want to emphasize, we need the Trump voters to come out, and that would be my appeal tonight.”

Pressed on areas of disagreement with Trump, Marshall said he called Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin after September immigration raids in southwest Kansas to say, “I don't think this is quite right, what's going on?”

He also cited his opposition to Trump opening up beef imports.

“Just like with my wife, I can disagree with her,” Marshall said. “Now, my wife is always right, and President Trump is not always right. But I do think it's great that I have a relationship, that I can pick up the phone and discuss with him the pros and cons of what he's contemplating.”

Marshall invoked Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer 17 times in the hour-long debate, pleading with his state’s conservative electorate to turn out and prevent the Senate from falling into Democratic control.

“Every Democrat stands up, and when Schumer tells them to jump, they say, ‘How high?’” Marshall said. “So why is [Hamilton] going to be any different once he gets to Washington?”

Hamilton, who considered running as an independent, is pitching himself as a moderate and trying to distance himself from the national Democratic brand. In the debate, he called former President Joe Biden’s border policies “a terrible disaster,” reminded viewers that he has said he wouldn’t support Schumer for majority leader and said he has “a lot of Trump supporters who are supporting me as well, which has been very exciting.”

“I just want to say, I'm not running against President Trump,” Hamilton said after criticizing the president’s decision to go to war with Iran. “I'm running against [Marshall], and he supported it again and again and again.”
entries.author: Hunter Riggall

entries.title: AIPAC Will Stop Endorsing Candidates, Focus on Super PAC Spending
entries.summary: AIPAC PAC will stop donating directly to candidates, though the organization will continue to use its United Democracy Project super PAC.
entries.content:
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee told its members Wednesday that the group will take a step back from directly endorsing and earmarking funds for candidates through its traditional political action committee, while leaving the group’s larger super PAC spending operation intact.

The group’s mission — boosting candidates who champion the U.S.-Israel partnership — has turned politically sour across the political aisle: Many have faced scrutiny for accepting AIPAC money, and some even rejected or returned contributions from the committee. AIPAC has spent more than $91 million this year between AIPAC PAC, the organization’s traditional committee, and United Democracy Project, the group’s super PAC.

AIPAC notified its members about the change in a letter, first reported by Jewish Insider, after a monthslong period of strategic review.

“We will prioritize increasing direct, organized contributions from individual Americans to candidates — expanding upon our current efforts — and maximizing the emerging political fundraising tools,” the letter, written by AIPAC’s board of directors, says. “Endorsements, direct PAC contributions, and earmarking will no longer be part of our approach so we can expand individual giving and utilize new tools to help our friends win.”

Bernie Kaminetsky, AIPAC’s president, and several other organization leaders signed onto the correspondence sent out to the group’s members Wednesday.

The organization has been financially active on behalf of political candidates for three congressional cycles. AIPAC PAC, which can donate up to $5,000 to a candidate under Federal Election Commission rules, will no longer make direct contributions. The group will continue to use its United Democracy Project super PAC, which can accept unlimited donations and contribute unlimited amounts to campaigns, in future elections.

“We’ve seen a surge of new fundraising strategies that have changed how candidates raise and utilize resources,” AIPAC’s leaders wrote in the letter. “These new models were inconceivable five years ago when we launched the AIPAC PAC and present significant opportunities for our community to help pro-Israel candidates win their races.”

The committee’s members donated more than $90 million directly to candidates this midterm cycle, AIPAC spokesperson Deryn Sousa wrote in a statement to The Washington Sun, adding that the “organized, direct giving from our members will continue and increase.”

“Our mission and strategy remain the same,” Sousa said. “Our goal is to build support for the U.S.-Israel relationship.”

Sousa told The Sun that the AIPAC community is “looking to dramatically expand” its political involvement and described the United Democracy Project as “one of the most important tools that AIPAC members use and will continue to use to help defeat anti-Israel candidates.”

Democrats’ opinions on Israel’s actions in Palestinian territory soured in a transformational way for the party this year: Many left-leaning progressives, particularly Democratic Socialist of America-backed candidates who often strongly reject U.S. military aid to Israel, used their opponents’ connections to AIPAC as an attack strategy on the campaign trail and to stand out during primary season.

The letter acknowledged that AIPAC helped “290 pro-Israel candidates win their elections and helped defeat 29 detractors” this campaign cycle “in one of the most challenging environments in recent memory.”

AIPAC sent a last-minute $9 million donation to Republican Mike Rogers in his competitive race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for Senate in Michigan, The New York Times reported Wednesday. Rogers had initially been hesitant to tie himself to AIPAC this campaign cycle, but the committee’s support contrasts with El-Sayed’s criticism of the U.S. government’s continued financial and military backing of Israel.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Trump Props Up Graham in Last-Minute Push in South Carolina Senate Race
entries.summary: Democrat Annie Andrews said Graham's need for Trump's visit shows she's losing.
entries.content:
By Meg Kinnard and Michelle L. Price

PENDLETON, S.C. — President Donald Trump traveled to South Carolina on Wednesday to boost U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, whose stumbles in her first campaign since replacing her late brother have Democratic voters hopeful — but not necessarily optimistic — that their candidate can break Republicans' grip on the state.

Trump, who was repeatedly interrupted by protesters early in his speech, sought to reassure South Carolinians on Wednesday that the late Sen. Lindsey Graham held his sister in high esteem. “Everybody respects her. She’s smart and incredible. She’ll never let you down,” Trump said as he made a case for her.

He said Graham's Democratic opponent, pediatrician Annie Andrews, would "be the most extreme and one of the most crazy people in the entire country. It would be a disaster.”

The president initially focused his remarks along Republican attack lines that accuse Andrews of supporting surgeries for transgender minors, which she denies. But the president over an hour and a half drifted from subject to subject, spending relatively little time on South Carolina.

Instead, he mused about renaming bodies of water, lamented that he should have won the Nobel Prize and the Pulitzer Prize, and did an imitation of a female bodybuilder. He ticked through some of the things he has done since returning to office, like his push to lower drug prices, and some goals for the rest of his term, such as expanding the death penalty.

Although South Carolina is not typically a midterm battleground, Trump has been deeply invested in Graham. He supported her appointment to replace Lindsey Graham after his death in July, and he backed her in a special primary when she faced several more experienced Republican opponents. But some distance emerged between the Republican president and the senator over the weekend over his decision to waive Ukraine war sanctions on Russia that were set to be imposed under a law named after Lindsey Graham.

Republicans want to make sure Andrews doesn't pull off an upset victory. More than $34 million has flowed into the race, and Republicans have hammered Andrews as a “radical liberal."

Trump this week is rallying every day for candidates across the country, even in conservative areas, and imploring voters to “pretend I'm on the ballot” in hopes of averting a lackluster midterm turnout for Republicans.

“Darline Graham knows that our campaign’s momentum is so strong she called Donald Trump to come campaign for her in South Carolina," Andrews said in a fundraising appeal email.

Darline Graham rushed to define herself — and clung close to Trump

Lindsey Graham had been on a glide path to a fifth term when he died of an aortic tear. Darline Graham, former director of the state agency for the blind, received bipartisan support when she was appointed to serve out her brother's term. But her decision to run for the seat in the midterms prompted skepticism that the political neophyte was up for the job.

Darline Graham had the endorsement of Trump, who campaigned for her before the runoff with U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman. A stumble over a question related to U.S. policy in Taiwan, in which Graham admitted she was “not that informed on national security,” prompted questions over her readiness.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who is from South Carolina and spoke ahead of Trump on Wednesday, said Graham was driven by the same kind of hope for America that her brother was.

“As long as Donald Trump is in the White House, and Darline Graham is in the Senate, we can all hope for a better country," he said.

Waiting for her at a weekend event in Mount Pleasant, Nanette Tumbleston said she felt strongly Graham should win, shuddering to think of what might happen if the seat fell to Democrats.

“I hope that everybody’s eyes will be open and we’ll have a Republican win," Tumbleston said, adding that she feared progressives' influence in the Democratic Party. “I just can’t see how they can see that the world’s going to be a better place with those policies.”

Andrews pivoted from Lindsey Graham to Darline Graham

Andrews launched her campaign more than a year before Lindsey Graham's death. She pivoted to criticizing Darline Graham as “Trump-endorsed and unqualified.”

Andrews argues that Republican policies have weakened not only the broader U.S. economy but also the financial situations of children and families, centering her message on “building a South Carolina that we can all afford,” as she said last week in Columbia.

As the pediatrician seemed to gain steam this fall, Republican groups infused millions of dollars into the race, characterizing the spending as an insurance policy for Graham. Trump attacked Andrews on social media, saying the Democrat doesn’t represent “the Values of the Great People of South Carolina.”

Some Andrews supporters acknowledge that while Democrats might ultimately break through in South Carolina, it might take more time.

Paul Davis, of Aiken, said “people are really angry and fed up, and they can’t afford things.” However, he said a Democratic victory “may be a cycle or two away.”

The candidates accuse each other of being unqualified

At their only debate, Graham and Andrews disagreed on issues including healthcare but primarily accused each other of inexperience.

“It is nothing personal, but she has shown time and time again that she is not up for the job,” Andrews said, calling Graham's interim appointment “a nice gesture."

Graham said serving while processing her brother's death showed “just how strong I am,” adding that ”I’m just as qualified as you are.”

At the Columbia rally, some of Andrews' supporters said they were hopeful, despite Democrats' years of Senate losses in the state. When Lindsey Graham last ran in 2020, he defeated Democrat Jaime Harrison by 10 percentage points in a contest that turned into South Carolina’s most expensive ever.

“It’s definitely frustrating," said Emily Glenham, a Columbia copywriter. "It’s definitely been disappointing, but you can’t not have hope.”

Sandra Martin, of West Columbia, agreed Andrews had “a good chance” but looked more toward the future.

“Georgia did it,” she said. “If Georgia can do it, there’s no reason we can’t, someday.”

___

Price reported from Washington.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: The Revamped Wizards Open Their Season With a Win Over the Bucks
entries.summary: Anthony Davis scored 34 points and got plenty of help as Washington beat Milwaukee, 128-116.
entries.content:
Bub Carrington was in unfamiliar territory.

In the second quarter of the Wizards’ 128-116 win over the Milwaukee Bucks on Wednesday, the third-year guard found himself sharing the floor with Anthony Davis, Khris Middleton, Trae Young and Deandre Ayton — Washington’s four most established veterans.

For those counting, that’s three All-Stars, two NBA champions and a former No. 1 overall pick. And yet, in those shared minutes, Carrington was the star.

“They have been playing basketball for a combined 100 years, if you want to add those four together,” Carrington told The Sun. “They literally know where to be at all times to make the game as easy as possible for everyone. It makes the game super easy for me. I run around like a chicken with my head cut off and fall into buckets.”

The 21-year-old hit a three to beat the shot clock, dished an assist to Davis and grabbed a quick steal. He finished the night with 10 points off the bench, providing the kind of performance the Wizards are hoping for as they blend a young core with a new cast of vets and look to compete in a way they haven’t for some time.

“Those guys have been in the wars, they’ve seen the battles,” Wizards coach Brian Keefe said of his veterans. “I think our guys are ready for the jump to join in with them. And you saw that tonight.”

Playing his first game in nine months, Davis reminded the fans why he’s considered one of the 75 greatest players in league history. He scored 34 points, 18 of which came in a third quarter when the Wizards’ offense was otherwise nonexistent.

Davis said Carrington came to him in the middle of a timeout early in the third quarter with the Wizards trailing.

“You have one more gear,” Carrington told him. “Can I see it?”

Davis’ performance even garnered a few “MVP” chants from a giddy home crowd. Davis, who hasn’t been award-eligible since 2024 because of numerous injuries, looked motivated Wednesday night despite offseason speculation about his contract situation and his future on a young Wizards team.

But while the Wizards got the job done, they also showed some of the disconnect that can be expected from a revamped roster. Errant passes were thrown, players were caught out of position and there was not an abundance of on-court chemistry.

Young had 20 points but struggled to find a rhythm, missing all six of his shots from 3. Most notably, he dished out a game-high 13 assists and had just one turnover. Washington had eight players score 8 or more points, a balanced approach that helped them overcome a 1-for-12 start from deep.

Kyshawn George chipped in 18 points and Bilal Coulibaly, who on Monday failed to reach an extension on his rookie contract, finished with 11. AJ Dybantsa, the biggest prize of the Wizards’ recent tanking, watched the win from the sidelines. He is still considered day-to-day with Washington hosting the Toronto Raptors on Friday.

“I think a lot of people [saw] tonight that even without AJ, we’re a different ball club this year,” Davis said.
entries.author: Alex Schiffer

entries.title: The NFL’s Top 5 Super Bowl Contenders So Far This Season
entries.summary: How the 49ers, Bills and others have separated themselves from the pack so far this season.
entries.content:
Bill Belichick once said you don’t know your team until the middle of October.

Well, here we are.

After six weeks, we’re starting to get a sense of who each team is and which teams have the best shot at winning it all this season. While there is still plenty of time for things to change before the end of the regular season, these five teams have established themselves as the league’s top Super Bowl contenders.

All stats per TruMedia unless noted otherwise.

San Francisco 49ers (6-0 record)

Why they’re contenders: This is one of the most well-rounded teams in the league. The 49ers are first in offensive DVOA and third in defensive DVOA through six weeks, per FTN.

Offensively, coach Kyle Shanahan and quarterback Brock Purdy have the passing game buzzing. Purdy is third among quarterbacks in expected points added (EPA) per play and has been the league’s best quarterback at sack avoidance. That’s allowed him to find open receivers all over the field. His immediate chemistry with Mike Evans unlocked a new element for the San Francisco passing game, with a ball-dominant outside receiver who has drawn coverage away from the likes of tight end George Kittle and running back Christian McCaffrey.

The defense has been one of the best at limiting big plays with an opposing explosive play rate of 7.1%, which is second to only the Seahawks.

At 6-0, FTN’s DVOA-based playoff odds give the 49ers a 30.8% chance to win the Super Bowl.

Concern: The injuries keep piling up. The 49ers were already thin at wide receiver and then Evans left Monday night’s game with an Achilles injury that had been bothering him before the game. He’s expected to miss time. The Niners passed on placing pass rusher Nick Bosa on injured reserve earlier in the season because they were already running out of spots to designate for return.

Kansas City Chiefs (5-0)

Why they’re contenders: There’s finally a dynamic run element to complement quarterback Patrick Mahomes and the passing game. When Kenneth Walker III was signed in free agency, the hope was that he could add explosives in a run game that has been without juice for years. He’s exceeded all expectations.

Last season, the Chiefs had one run from a running back gain at least 20 yards. This year, they lead the league with seven through six weeks. Walker leads the league in rushing yards, but is also first in EPA per rush (0.15) and third in success rate (48.1%) among running backs with at least 50 carries.
Kenneth Walker (4614x3076, AR: 1.50)Teams don’t need a successful run game to use play-action effectively, but being able to get under center has opened things up for the Kansas City passing game. Mahomes has a league-high 33.7% play-action rate, which would be a career high if it holds. He’s fourth in EPA per play this season.

Concern: With the loss of receiver Tyquan Thornton to an ankle injury, the Chiefs might not have the vertical element to threaten opposing defenses — a problem with the Kansas City passing offense for the past few years. With Thornton on the field, Mahomes averaged 9.2 yards per attempt, but that drops to 7.2 without him.

Buffalo Bills (5-1)

Why they’re contenders: The Buffalo offense is a machine, whether it’s Josh Allen doing Josh Allen things at quarterback or a run game that can be used to control the clock. Against the Raiders in Week 6, the Bills had 10 offensive drives and scored on 70% of them. That had been done only one other time this season … by the Bills in Week 5 against the Rams.

Buffalo is averaging 3.13 points per drive, the fourth-best mark for a team through Week 6 since 2020.

The Bills have leaned into heavier personnel with their 28.7% rate of 13 personnel (one running back, three tight ends), second behind the Rams. The bigger bodies and wider fronts have helped open up running lanes for James Cook, who leads the league in yards before contact per rush at 2.47, over half a yard above the next-best running back.

Concern: The defense has struggled under new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. Leonhard was expected to bring some more exotic looks and simulated pressures, but early in the season, he’s simplified some of his defense due to a lack of talent, especially in the secondary. The Bills are 32nd in points per drive allowed on defense.

Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2)

Why they’re contenders: Things have clicked for Trevor Lawrence under coach Liam Coen. The quarterback has carried the success he had during the second half of last season into the start of this year. He ranks fifth among QBs in EPA per play and 10th in success rate. He’s targeting the intermediate middle of the field — the most valuable area by expected points — at a significantly higher rate than the rest of the league (17.9%, with the next-highest quarterback at 12.6%).

Parker Washington has emerged as a legitimate No.1 wide receiver, who ranks 14th at the position in yards per route run.

Concern: This is kind of a sloppy team. The Jaguars have four delay-of-game penalties, and could’ve had more if not for some burned timeouts. They also have 13 offensive holding penalties. Only the Chargers have lost more offensive EPA to penalties than the Jaguars this season.

Minnesota Vikings (5-0)

Why they’re contenders: The Vikings have the league’s best defense by DVOA on the back of the most aggressive front in the league. Minnesota has blitzed on 66.5% of opposing dropbacks this season, easily the most over a team’s first five games since 2019. The next-closest team was the 2023 Vikings at 55%.

But a big difference is how often this Minnesota team is creating pressure. The 2023 Vikings only had a 29.5% pressure rate, while this year’s version leads the league with a 44.9% pressure rate. It’s not just about the blitzes, either. The Vikings have the highest pressure rate with a four-man rush, at 56.4%.

When the Vikings have gotten pressure, they have allowed a league-low 2.1 yards per play.

Concern: The offense has yet to click. Quarterback Kyler Murray has played only three full games, and just one with star receiver Justin Jefferson, which was his best. The run game also hasn’t taken shape and the offense as a whole ranks 27th in DVOA.

entries.title: Abdul El-Sayed Wants MAHA Voters
entries.summary: Some of the Michigan Democrat’s proposals align with RFK Jr.’s MAHA movement. But El-Sayed’s nonnegotiables complicate his pitch.
entries.content:
MUSKEGON, Mich. — John Trocke is at a place he’s never been before: considering whether to vote for a Democrat. Specifically, Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

The 42-year-old architect from Holland, Michigan, has been frustrated with the Trump administration’s failure to adopt the majority of Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again platform.

“Republicans need to be spanked a bit in this coming midterm,” Trocke said. “I've become so disenchanted with the GOP that I've opened myself … to different possibilities.”

Trocke is one of a growing cadre of MAHA voters around the nation who say the Trump administration has failed to make good on the promises of the 2024 presidential race. He’s also part of a voting bloc that El-Sayed believes he can lure away from Republicans.

El-Sayed’s platform, which includes several policies aligned closely with MAHA priorities on food quality, pesticides and breaking apart monopolies in America’s food system, has interested Trocke, who already supported El-Sayed’s views on Iran and Israel.

“I think [RFK Jr.] has sold out his movement,” El-Sayed said in an interview with The Washington Sun on Monday. The former Wayne County health director added that he worked on and wrote about these issues before Robert F. Kennedy Jr. ran for president.

“I want to be talking about what we can actually do to take that mantle, [and] stand up against corporations,” El-Sayed said.

MAHA supporters never cleanly fit in either party. Kennedy, who himself was a longtime Democrat before 2023, helped Republicans expand their tent to include voters motivated by environmental and wellness causes, including anti-vaccine activists.

But the MAHA movement has been hot and cold on Republicans’ record. The administration began to phase out synthetic red food coloring and scaled back childhood vaccines, but the MAHA movement is still frustrated that President Donald Trump and Kennedy haven’t done more to go after food conglomerates and were deeply critical of Trump’s decision to loosen regulations on pesticides and other chemicals.

Whether that anger gives candidates like El-Sayed a shot at more votes depends on what these MAHA voters want to prioritize — and whether they’re willing to fully turn against Kennedy.

“RFK Jr. is kind of one of our iconic leaders,” said Rachel Atwood, an organizer in Western Michigan’s MAHA community who likes El-Sayed’s position on banning pesticides, but says she’s still likely to vote for Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers. “Can [El-Sayed] win over MAHA voters based on dyes and pesticides when he has now … verbalized support of vaccine [mandates] and has attacked RFK Jr. for questioning them?”

El-Sayed has nonnegotiables. He’s adamant about vaccines and is a sharp critic of Kennedy’s. He accused the health secretary of being “bought by corporations” in his interview with The Sun, and promised to open an investigation into how the Department of Health and Human Services handled the recent cyclospora outbreak if appointed to the Senate committee overseeing HHS.

“Eight thousand Michiganders were infected, and possibly, probably many, many more,” El-Sayed said of the outbreak. “I really want to subpoena him and understand why this happened.”

El-Sayed’s position on vaccines was a deal-breaker for Atwood.

For Trocke, who is vaccinated and aligns more with the anti-pesticide side of RFK’s platform, El-Sayed could do more to soften his approach toward Kennedy.

“If he were to even express some magnanimous attitude towards RFK himself,” Trocke said, “I think that would be a positive thing, and would certainly be appealing to those of us who were in that RFK camp.”

El-Sayed told The Sun he is willing to work with the health secretary — between the subpoenas.

“Where we can work together to serve Michiganders, we will, and where I need to hold him accountable to serve Michiganders, I will,” he said.

If he makes it to Washington in January, El-Sayed said he would also reach out to HHS to probe Kennedy’s leadership.

“I know for sure that there are a lot of people who work underneath [RFK Jr.] who are so disaffected by him and his leadership style,” El-Sayed said. “I will be having those conversations.”

El-Sayed says the strongest policy overlaps between his health platform and the existing MAHA movement center on processed foods and monopolies. Monopolies in America’s food system would be his first point of attack if elected to the Senate.

But while health is a regular focus of El-Sayed’s campaign stops — his calls for single-payer Medicare received some of the loudest cheers of the night at a recent town hall in Muskegon — the Democrat’s stump speech doesn’t always champion the more MAHA-coded policies in his platform.

Tasha Schurgin, a longtime organizer with Michigan for Vaccine Choice, believes El-Sayed is simply throwing the MAHA community crumbs to gain their vote.

“If you're going to say, ‘Hey, I support the MAHA movement,’ you've got to really support it wholeheartedly. You can't pick and choose what you want to support,” said Schurgin, who lives in the greater Detroit area and considers vaccines her top issue. She is voting for Rogers, who she calls the lesser of two evils.

“By no means do I think Mike Rogers is a champion of the MAHA movement or vaccine choice,” she said. “But I don't also see him trying to capitalize on it and be a wolf in sheep's clothing.”

The Rogers campaign did not return a request for comment.

Atwood points out, however, that factions of the MAHA movement still have the potential to be swayed by El-Sayed’s policies.

Trocke falls into that category. He voted for Trump in 2016 but left the presidential race blank on his ballot in the last two elections. RFK’s support for Trump in 2024 nearly lured him back to vote for the president, but this year, he has already decided he will not vote for Mike Rogers.

He’s still undecided, though, on whether he will vote for El-Sayed or leave that part of the ballot blank.

“Policy statements are easy to print and produce,” Trocke said. “But I think it certainly appears to be a good step that he came out with something.”

entries.title: Natural Gas Will Be Used at RFK Stadium — Just for Cooking and Heating
entries.summary: Officials say there won’t be a gas-fired power plant built, but some community members remain skeptical.
entries.content:
A natural gas-fired power plant won’t be built as part of the 180-acre redevelopment of the RFK Stadium Campus, officials said Wednesday following a flurry of activity from community and environmental organizers who worried that project leaders could be walking back some green energy commitments.

In a statement to The Washington Sun on Wednesday, a spokesperson from the RFK Project Management Office said “there is no need for, nor will there be, a natural gas-fired power plant” as part of the $3.8 billion project. Along with new green space and parks, the RFK Campus Master Plan calls for over 5,500 new housing units, with 30% of them to be dedicated as affordable. The redevelopment is expected to bring over $4 billion in new tax revenue and create 2,000 permanent jobs, according to the master plan.

Though no power plant is planned, natural gas is expected to be used in the project regardless — just to keep fans warm and cook their hot dogs come opening day, a Washington Commanders official said Wednesday. Given the size and scale of the project, using “minimal” natural gas for heating and cooking would be required because of power capacity and to stay on track for a 2030 opening.

The use of natural gas in the project will require an exemption to the Greener Government Buildings Amendment Act of 2022, which forbids the use of fossil fuels in publicly funded projects. The exemption would be reviewed by the Green Building Advisory Council.

On Wednesday, a coalition of nonprofits and neighborhood organizations held a press conference to denounce the idea of building a new gas-fired power plant at the site. Attendees held signs stating, “GAS at RFK = POISON to people + planet” and “Burning gas at RFK? It’s a trick play. Block it.”

It still feels “very unclear what the plan is,” Mark Rodeffer, the political committee chair for the Sierra Club of the District of Columbia, said Wednesday. While officials have indicated they are not planning a power plant, a March request for proposals for an RFK redevelopment energy plan indicated a contractor would evaluate “the integration of a combined heat and power natural gas facility” in the RFK redevelopment.

Even if a natural gas facility is not included in the plan, Rodeffer said it was “outrageous” that a request to evaluate integrating one was in the RFP. The final energy plan is yet to be released. Officials have also complicated the language used to refer to the energy plan.

During a Sept. 30 hearing, Department of Buildings Director Brian Hanlon said that a natural gas power plant was “not under consideration,” but also said there would be a blended solution of “electricity to the stadium and natural gas systems” in order to open by 2030. Many attendees at the October press conference, like Rodeffer, had expressed concerns about the project during the hearing.

The final energy plan is expected to conclude later this year, which would coincide with a plan to hire an energy developer, Hanlon said during the hearing.

entries.title: Former DHS Data Chief: White House’s Tally of Immigrants Leaving Is ‘Highly Unlikely’
entries.summary: The Trump administration says 3 million immigrants left the U.S., but it has not explained how it reached that number.
entries.content:
A former top statistics official who resigned from the Department of Homeland Security this summer says the government is overstating how many unauthorized immigrants have left the country during President Donald Trump’s second term.

Marc Rosenblum, whose blistering resignation letter from a decade-long career at DHS garnered national attention, is behind a new estimate published Thursday that says between 790,000 and 1.9 million immigrants departed the U.S. from Jan. 20, 2025, to July 31, 2026.

The Trump administration has said more than 3 million unauthorized immigrants have left during that period, but has not explained how it reached the number. The new analysis from the Migration Policy Institute, a think tank where Rosenblum is now a senior fellow, is an attempt to fill in the gap of information left by DHS’s lack of reporting.

“It's highly unlikely that 3 million total foreign-born [people] departed the United States in the first 18 months of the Trump administration, and even more unlikely that 3 million unauthorized immigrants departed during that time period,” Rosenblum said.

MPI’s analysis didn’t include immigrants who had lived in the U.S. less than a year because that wouldn’t match the common understanding of what it means to reduce the size of the unauthorized population, Rosenblum said.

The think tank said its estimate increases to 1.3 million to 2.4 million total departures — still short of the government’s number — when accounting for those who had been present in the country less than a year, as well as people turned around at the border without setting foot inside the U.S., whom the government does include in its count.

Rosenblum said DHS counts people who were turned aside at border entry points before entering the country as well as those who overstay visas by a few days. And the government doesn’t gather data on most people who leave the U.S. through the southern border, he said.

Researchers lack information about how the government counts that 3 million number. Republican lawmakers and immigration hawks have called for transparency from DHS, wanting to see the results of Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts.

The White House once again touted on Tuesday the more than 3 million departures, saying in a press release that it has deported or removed nearly 1.2 million immigrants living in the U.S. illegally. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said deportations are at a record high.

Although MPI’s analysis contests the department’s accounting of total departures, the think tank concluded that the number of immigrants who left was two to three times higher than in the past 12 years.

“Most of the numbers are not at all-time highs,” Rosenblum said.

Among other data, MPI used information forced out of the administration through public records lawsuits from the Deportation Data Project and Mexican census data capturing the number of the country’s nationals who returned after living in the U.S.

DHS hasn’t been responsive to requests for immigration enforcement data from the Oversight Project, a group that supports the president’s crackdown on illegal immigration and has filed two lawsuits demanding records on deportations and self-deportations.

“I have no reason to doubt the 3 million figures, but also have no reason to believe it until they release the actual data,” said Neal Cornett, the project’s director of state litigation. “It's just a claim from the Department of Homeland Security, and there should be data that they would have that would be able to confirm that.”

The Oversight Project requested records showing the number of immigrants who have self-deported via a Customs and Border Protection app and the amount of money DHS has spent on stipends for those immigrants, according to documents Cornett shared with The Washington Sun.

DHS gave the group an entirely redacted document on Oct. 8. The department claimed the records were protected under exemptions that shield law enforcement information that “would disclose techniques and procedures for law enforcement investigation or prosecution,” according to a letter DHS sent to the Oversight Project.

“It's not like we're asking the exact details of it, or how these people would be contacting them or anything like that,” Cornett said. “We just want to know what the numbers are.”

A White House spokesperson referred questions to DHS, which did not respond to requests for comment.
